Most people who have heard of usenet these days, probably have the idea that it's a complicated filesharing system. I think the various groups who are associated with owning and moderating most popular forums, such as reddit, are only to happy to let that image persist. The truth is that USENET was once much more than a second rate filesharing tool. It used to be the best persistent discussion forum yet conceived by man. Sometimes, it still is. And it can be again.

I could write a long post detailing all of the advantages a system like usenet has over sites like reddit, web forums, *chans, and journals(if anyone wants me to, I will, I'd like to spark some discussion and hopefully get some critiques). Those advantages persist, and right now I think usenet's main problem is it's perception. There's nothing wrong with usenet being a filesharing system, of course. But we need to fight the perception that that's all it is, and all it can be.

If you were around during the late 90's, when usenet as a discussion system was dying, I think that just about everyone who was involved with usenet at more than a superficial level recognized what was killing usenet. Although opinions differed, most people seemed to finger one or more of the following as the problem:

  1. Spam: Very simply, usenet was being drowned by a tidal wave of spam. This was probably the biggest problem. It ate up bandwidth, it taxed administrators time, and it obscured legitimate content.

  2. Stealth Binaries Groups: another huge problem, this ate up even MORE bandwidth, taxed the infrastructure, and often concealed dubious or illegal content. Furthermore, it discouraged administrators from carrying groups(particularly in the alt* hierarchy) that they couldn't be sure wouldn't be used for off-topic binaries.

  3. Deliberate obfuscation: Most ISPs hated USENET. It was hard to manage, didn't bring them any income, and this was exacerbated by the prior two issues. And they weren't the only ones who didn't like it. The developing web forums of the time competed with it for users and content, and Google and the other major search engines of the time didn't like it much either, because it was, and is, so damn hard to monetize. This culminated with Google buying out Dejanews, turning it into Google Groups, and then deliberately running it into the ground at a million miles an hour. Around the same time, ISPs stopped carrying usenet by default, often using the excuse of illegal filesharing as justification. Prior to that, guides on setting up usenet had disappeared from ISP's and universities default introductions.

  4. Improvements in webforums: There's really little of value that webforums have that usenet, with the right readers and servers, couldn't do just as well. Except maybe moderating, controlling, tracking and monetizing it's users. The problem is that even though usenet could in theory have kept up with whatever features appealed to people, there was little standardization, and even relatively simple features like inline links and media took quite a while to get out, let alone in a standardized form. And some people left due to flashy graphics, avatars, and links. How many is debateable, but to some extent it happened.

15 years later, things have changed. Spamfighting and detection algorithms have improved. Bandwidth is cheap. Word of mouth, strategically used, is a powerful as ever. ** And the world is more than ever in need of a resilient, open system for discussion, one that isn't controlled by a single entity with financial or political motivations.**
USENET is more than a filesharing system. We should bring it back.

The main thing that "killed" usenet - stupid people who only started using the internet after the web had been developed, and demanded every service to be provided over it rather than use the services (usenet, ftp, irc etc) that already did a far better job than the web could manage.

That, and the fact that there was money to be made from ad banners on the web.

Sad that people abandoned ready made services that worked better, all for a perceived ease of use.
